deep.reconstruction:
Context: the 1983 'Teichmüller' notes that later became the 'Teichmüller Lego' / Teichmüller tower of the Esquisse d'un programme (1984). Grothendieck is studying the small modular surfaces of modular dimension 1, types (0,4) and (1,1), through 'canonical maps' (cartes): cell structures on the punctured surface determined by highly symmetric conformal structures. The previous page dealt with the square and hexagonal tori (automorphism groups mu_4 and mu_6) and the tetrahedral/octahedral maps. The next page lists the basic pieces: A, of type (0,3), d=0; T, the oriented trihedron, of type (0,4), d=1; Q, of type (1,1); and the oriented tori E_Q and E_H.

This page:
(1) Many sketches of spheres with 3 or 4 holes, carrying trivalent graphs, pants curves and a tetrahedral graph drawn on the sphere. The four holes are labelled a, b, c, d. There is a 1-simplex sketch '0 —— 1'.
(2) A large sketch of the 4-holed sphere with a meridian/equator cell structure and points marked (apparently) -1, 1/2 and so on. An arrow leads to a sphere with three marked holes on the equator, which reads as a model of M_{0,4} = P^1 - {0,1,inf} with its special points.
(3) Top right: a quadrilateral Q with its two diagonals, and the formulas diag_Q ≅ omega_Q and diag_Q ⊗ omega_Q ≅ codiag_Q. In modern terms: for a quadrilateral, i.e. a 4-holed sphere with its two pants decompositions related by an elementary move, the two-element set of 'diagonals' is a torsor. Tensoring with the orientation torsor omega_Q exchanges diagonal and codiagonal. This encodes that a quarter-turn of an oriented square swaps the diagonals.
(4) Middle-right text, roughly: 'with a set I of three elements, one makes 3×2 = 6 certain [maps] of type (1,1)'. This is presumably level-2 structures, i.e. labellings of the three nonzero 2-torsion points by I, on the special tori. This links M_{1,1}[2] with M_{0,4}.
(5) Bottom text: 'with a set I of card 4 one can find 17 canonical maps of type (0,4) (17 = 3×4 + 3 + 2): two tetrahedra, three squares, 2×3 = 6 assemblies of two right T's, 2×3 = 6 assemblies of left T's.'

Interpretation and check of the count. M_{0,4} with labelled points is Gamma(2)\H, of index 6 in PSL_2(Z).
- The labelled tetrahedra are the equianharmonic configurations, lambda = e^{±i pi/3}. There are 4!/|A_4| = 2 of them.
- The labelled squares are the harmonic configurations, lambda in {-1, 2, 1/2}. There are 4!/|D_4| = 3 of them.
- The 12 = 6 + 6 'T-assemblies' match the 12 triangles of the (2,3,inf) tessellation of Gamma(2)\H, in two chiralities. Check: area 2pi divided by the triangle area pi/6 gives 12; equivalently, the 6 edges of the modular dessin, doubled by orientation.
So 2 + 3 + 12 = 17. The page is a census of the cells of the canonical (extended-modular) cell decomposition of M_{0,4}, with chirality kept track of. It is an explicit worked example of the 'canonical cell decomposition of modular multiplicities via maps' that the Esquisse announces in general.
errors: The text first wrote 14 and corrected it to 17. The decomposition 3×4 + 3 + 2 = 17 is internally consistent with the itemised list 6 + 6 + 3 + 2.

No mathematical error is visible. The interpretation of the 'T-assemblies' as the chiral 2-cells of the (2,3,inf) tessellation is my reconstruction, not stated on the page. The edges (18 of them) and the cusps are not counted, so 'canonical maps' presumably means the 0-cells and 2-cells only.

ideas.what: Census of the canonical maps of type (0,4) with labelled points: 2 tetrahedral, 3 square, 12 chiral 'T-assemblies'.
ideas.modern_name: Cells of the (2,3,inf)/extended-modular tessellation of M_{0,4} = Gamma(2)\H; equianharmonic and harmonic points; dessin of the modular curve X(2).
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical (Klein, Fricke) for the tessellation; the 'Lego' viewpoint to Grothendieck (Esquisse 1984); ribbon-graph cell decompositions to Harer, Penner, Kontsevich, Strebel.
ideas.where_published: The Esquisse d'un programme discusses the Teichmüller Lego, the (0,4) and (1,1) pieces and cell decompositions via maps in general; this explicit count is not known to me in print.

ideas.what: Torsor identity diag_Q ⊗ omega_Q ≅ codiag_Q for a quadrilateral.
ideas.modern_name: Elementary (Hatcher–Thurston) move on a 4-holed sphere; orientation twisting exchanging the two pants decompositions.
ideas.usually_credited_to: Hatcher–Thurston (1980); Hatcher–Lochak–Schneps for the Lego formalism.

ideas.what: Level-2 labellings (3×2 = 6) of (1,1) maps by a 3-element set I.
ideas.modern_name: M_{1,1}[2] ≅ M_{0,4} (Legendre family); the 2-torsion points as a 3-element set.

missed.claim: An explicit worked enumeration (17 = 2 + 3 + 6 + 6) of canonical labelled maps on the 4-punctured sphere, distinguishing chiralities. It is a concrete instance of the cell structure underlying the Teichmüller Lego, apparently not printed in this form.
missed.quote: avec un ens. I de card 4, on peut trouver 17 cartes canoniques de type (0,4) (17 = 3×4 + 3 + 2) dont deux tétraèdres, trois carrés, 2×3 = 6 assemblages de 2 'T' droits, 6 = 2×3 assemblages de 'T' gauches
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Mainly historical: it documents how Grothendieck concretely built the dimension-1 Lego pieces (0,4) and (1,1) in 1983. The mathematics is classical.

deep.surprise_reason: A careful, correct but classical enumeration of the special points and chiral cells of M_{0,4}, part of the known Teichmüller-Lego programme. It is historically illustrative, but contains nothing a specialist would find new.
transcription_corrections: '14' is overwritten as 17; the parenthesis reads '(17 = 3×4 + 3 + 2)'.
'avec un cas I de card 4' should read 'avec un ens[emble] I de card 4'.
Middle-right text likely reads: 'avec un ens. I à trois éléments, on fait 3×2 = 6 cartes de type (1,1)'.
'ℂ^3' and 'ℂ^4' appear to be small hand-drawn loop/curve symbols with indices 3 and 4, not complex affine spaces.
Top right formulas: 'diag_Q ≅ omega_Q' and 'diag_Q ⊗ omega_Q ≅ codiag_Q'.
'Mireille & enfants' in the top-left margin is a personal note (presumably his ex-wife Mireille and their children), not mathematics.
